title: How to Save Money on Pizza Delivery: 11 Tactics
excerpt: Most advice about saving money on pizza is either obvious or wrong. Here are the eleven things that genuinely move the total, ranked by how much they save.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Photo for a guide about saving money on pizza delivery

pricing.label: Typical family delivery order
pricing.note: Two large pizzas, a side and a drink, including fees and a standard tip. The spread is what tactics on this page are worth.

faqs.question: What is the single biggest saving on a pizza order?
faqs.answer: Switching from delivery to carryout, if collecting is practical for you. It removes the delivery fee, the tip and usually unlocks a lower flat price on the pizza itself, which together is commonly eight to twelve dollars on a single-pizza order.

faqs.question: Do coupon codes still work at pizza chains?
faqs.answer: Increasingly the discounts are built into the site as deal tiles rather than typed codes. Both routes exist, but the deal tiles are where most of the value now sits, and they apply automatically when your basket qualifies.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to order two mediums or one large?
faqs.answer: One large is almost always more pizza per dollar than one medium, but two mediums under a flat-rate bundle can beat one large at menu price. The rule that holds is to compare price per square inch rather than price per pizza.

content:
There is a lot of advice about saving money on takeaway pizza and most of it is worth nothing. Telling someone to look for coupons is not advice; it is a description of wanting to spend less. What follows is the list we actually use, in the order of how much money each one saves on a typical order.

For context: across our sample of stores, a family delivery order of two large pizzas, a side and a drink comes to somewhere between thirty-four and fifty-two dollars depending entirely on how it is put together. That eighteen-dollar spread is the whole subject of this article. Nothing here involves eating less pizza.

1. Switch to carryout, when it is genuinely practical

This is the largest single saving available and it is not close. Collecting your own order removes the delivery fee, removes the tip, and — this is the part people miss — usually unlocks a separate, cheaper price on the pizza itself. Chains run flat-rate carryout offers that simply do not exist in delivery mode.

Add those three together on a single large pizza and you are frequently looking at eight to twelve dollars, which is most of the price of the pizza. The caveat is real, though: if collecting means a twenty-minute drive each way, you have spent forty minutes and a gallon of petrol to save nine dollars. Carryout wins when the store is close.

2. Price your basket both ways before you check out

Chains run two parallel pricing systems: menu prices, and deal prices. They are not the same items at different discounts — they are separate structures, and which one wins depends on what you are ordering.

A percentage-off code applied to menu prices beats a flat bundle when your order is large. A flat bundle beats a percentage when your order is small and includes cheap items. The only way to know is to build the basket twice, which takes ninety seconds and regularly finds four or five dollars.

3. Order the most expensive thing inside a flat-price deal

If an offer says any large pizza at a fixed price, that fixed price buys you a plain cheese pizza or a fully loaded meat pizza equally. One of those is a much better use of the money.

This sounds obvious written down. In practice, people default to ordering what they normally order and then apply whatever deal fits, rather than choosing the item that extracts the most from the deal. Reverse the order of those decisions.

4. Take the drinks off the order

Soft drinks from a pizza store cost roughly twice supermarket price. A two-litre bottle and a couple of individual drinks on a family order is five or six dollars of pure convenience charge, and it is the least painful thing on the list to remove because you are not giving up any food.

The exception is a bundle that includes the drink at no extra cost. Where that exists, take it.

5. Count your toppings before you check out

Build-your-own pizzas start cheap and get expensive fast, because each topping carries a charge that scales with pizza size. Somewhere around the third or fourth topping on a large, a specialty pizza with five toppings becomes cheaper than your custom one with four.

Almost nobody checks this at the point of ordering. It is worth thirty seconds of comparison every time.

6. Use the free modifications

Light sauce, extra sauce, light cheese, well-done bake, square cut instead of wedge cut — all free at most stores, all of which change the pizza. Extra cheese and extra meat are the paid ones. Knowing which is which means you can customise substantially without touching the price.

7. Sign in before you order, every time

Loyalty points do not attach to guest checkouts, and most schemes will not add them retrospectively. Every guest order is a small amount of free pizza thrown away.

Worth knowing: at most chains, carryout orders earn points at the same rate as delivery. People assume they do not and lose points on exactly the orders they should be placing.

8. Order early rather than at peak

This does not change the price directly, but it changes what you get for it. Placing an order at 6:30pm on a Friday puts you into the deepest part of the queue at every store in the country. The same order at 5:15pm arrives faster and in better condition, and you have paid the same money for a materially better product.

9. Scale up rather than adding items

Going from a medium to a large costs a few dollars and adds around sixty percent more pizza. Adding a second medium costs the full price of a second pizza. When feeding more people, the first move is always to increase size, not quantity.

10. Stop paying for wings as a main course

Wings are the worst food-per-dollar item on a pizza menu because a large share of the weight is bone. As a side for a table, fine. As the thing that feeds a person, a second pizza costs less and feeds more.

11. Tip on the driver, not on the total

This one is not about spending less — it is about spending it in the right place. The delivery fee is a store charge and, at most chains, does not reach the driver. Cutting the tip because a fee was already applied is a misunderstanding that costs the person who drove to your house.

If your budget is tight, cut the drinks and the extra cheese. Do not cut the tip.

Putting it together

The tactics stack. On the family order we priced at the top of this article, using carryout where practical, dropping the drinks, choosing the deal structure that suits the basket and putting the heaviest pizza into the flat-rate slot takes a fifty-dollar order to the mid-thirties without removing a single slice of pizza from the table.

None of it requires waiting for a special promotion or hunting for a code. It requires ordering deliberately rather than by habit, which is the only pizza-saving advice we would stand behind.

title: Carryout vs Delivery: The Real Cost Difference, Worked Out
excerpt: Everyone knows carryout is cheaper. Almost nobody knows by how much, or at what driving distance the saving stops being worth it. We did the arithmetic.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Photo comparing carryout and delivery pizza costs

pricing.label: Same large pizza, both ways
pricing.note: One large pizza on a carryout offer versus the same pizza delivered with fee and tip.

faqs.question: How much cheaper is carryout than delivery?
faqs.answer: On a single large pizza, commonly eight to twelve dollars once you account for the flat carryout price, the delivery fee and a standard tip. On a large multi-item order the gap narrows in percentage terms because the fee and tip are spread across more food.

faqs.question: Does the delivery fee go to the driver?
faqs.answer: At most chains, no. It is a store charge that covers insurance, vehicle costs and operational overhead. Drivers are paid a wage plus tips, which is why cutting the tip because a fee was charged hurts the driver rather than the company.

faqs.question: At what distance does carryout stop being worth it?
faqs.answer: Roughly at the point where the round trip exceeds fifteen to twenty minutes of driving. Beyond that, fuel and time consume the saving on a single-pizza order, though it can still make sense on a large one.

content:
Carryout is cheaper than delivery. That is not in dispute and it is not interesting. The useful questions are how much cheaper, why the gap is that size, and at what point driving to collect your own pizza stops making financial sense.

Delivery drivers we've talked to have plenty of opinions about the tip section further down this page. But the arithmetic at the top is just arithmetic.

Where the gap actually comes from

People assume the difference is the delivery fee. The fee is the smallest of three components.

Component one: the fee itself

Typically somewhere between three and six dollars depending on the market and your distance from the store. It is a store charge, not a driver payment — more on that below.

Component two: the tip

A standard tip on a single-pizza order is three to five dollars, and on a larger order proportionally more. This is a real cost of having food delivered even though it is technically discretionary.

Component three: the price of the pizza

This is the one people miss, and it is the largest. Chains run flat-rate carryout offers — a large pizza at a fixed price, any toppings — that have no delivery equivalent. The identical pizza can carry a menu price six or seven dollars higher when you are in delivery mode.

Stack all three and a single large pizza that costs around eight dollars collected can cost around twenty-one delivered. That is not a markup on delivery; it is three separate charges pointing in the same direction.

Why the pizza itself is priced differently

A carryout order costs the store almost nothing to fulfil beyond the food. Nobody drives anywhere, no vehicle is insured, no time is spent out of the building. A delivery order consumes fifteen to thirty minutes of a driver's shift.

Chains would rather you collected, and they price accordingly. The flat carryout rate is a discount to change your behaviour, not a reward for loyalty.

When delivery is the right call anyway

The saving is real, but it is not free. Here is when I would still pay it.

  • The store is more than ten minutes away. A twenty-minute round trip plus fuel eats most of a nine-dollar saving, and it costs you twenty minutes.
  • You are ordering a lot. On a fifty-dollar order the fee and tip are a smaller share of the total, and the flat carryout rate usually applies to one pizza rather than four.
  • Weather, or no car. In a Chicago February the calculation changes completely, and it should.
  • The food is temperature-sensitive. A lava cake or cheesy bread collected and eaten in ten minutes is better than the same item delivered. But a pizza in your own car for twenty minutes is not better than a pizza in an insulated bag for twenty-five.

The distance where it flips

Working from a nine-dollar saving on a single large pizza and rough vehicle running costs, the break-even lands somewhere around a fifteen to twenty minute round trip — and that is before you value your own time at anything.

Value your time at even ten dollars an hour and a twenty-minute round trip has consumed a third of the saving before you have bought any petrol. For a single pizza from a store fifteen minutes away, delivery is defensible. For a single pizza from a store four minutes away, carryout is close to free money.

The fee and the tip are not the same thing

This is the part I will not be neutral about.

At most chains the delivery fee does not go to the driver. It goes to the store, and it covers insurance, vehicle wear on company-owned cars, and general operating cost. Drivers typically receive a wage plus their tips, sometimes with a small per-run reimbursement that does not resemble the fee amount.

What that means practically: when someone sees a five-dollar delivery fee and reduces their tip because they feel they have already paid for delivery, the person absorbing that is the driver, not the chain. It is one of the most common misunderstandings in the whole business, and it is expensive for the people least able to absorb it.

If you want to spend less on a delivery order, cut the drinks, cut the extra cheese, order a bundle instead of menu items. There are half a dozen levers before you get to the tip.

Practical rules

  • Choose carryout or delivery before you build the basket. Carryout-only pricing does not appear if the site has you in delivery mode.
  • If you are collecting, put the most heavily topped pizza on the menu into the flat-rate slot.
  • If you are having it delivered, order in a way that spreads the fee across more food — one larger order beats two small ones.
  • Do not drive fifteen minutes each way to save nine dollars unless you wanted the drive anyway.

The short version

Carryout saves eight to twelve dollars on a single large pizza and less, proportionally, on a big order. It is worth doing when the store is close and not worth doing when it is not. And the delivery fee is not the tip, whatever the checkout screen implies by putting them next to each other.

title: The Best Pizza Deals Right Now (and How to Tell)
excerpt: Deals are designed to look bigger than they are. Here is how to read them properly, plus the offer types that consistently deliver real value.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Photo for a guide to the best current pizza deals

faqs.question: Which pizza deal type gives the best value?
faqs.answer: Flat-rate carryout offers on a single pizza give the biggest saving per item, while multi-item bundles give the lowest cost per person once you are feeding four or more. Which is best depends entirely on how many people you are feeding.

faqs.question: Do pizza deals change every month?
faqs.answer: The headline promotions rotate, but the underlying offer types are remarkably stable: a flat carryout price, a two-item bundle, a family pack and a percentage-off online discount are close to permanent fixtures with different names.

faqs.question: Can I stack more than one pizza deal?
faqs.answer: Rarely. Most chains explicitly prevent combining a percentage discount with a bundle price. The reliable approach is to price the basket under each offer separately and keep the cheaper result.

content:
Pizza deals are a marketing product before they are a discount. That is not cynicism — the offer that gets promoted hardest in any given month is the one the chain most wants you to order, which is not automatically the one that saves you the most money.

This guide is about reading them properly. The specific promotions rotate; the structures underneath them barely change from year to year, and once you can identify which structure you are looking at, evaluating it takes about ten seconds.

The five deal structures, and what each is good for

1. Flat-rate carryout on a single pizza

A large pizza, any toppings, at one fixed price if you collect it. This is the single largest per-item saving in the business, and it is the one to use when you are feeding one or two people.

The trick: because the price is fixed regardless of toppings, ordering the most heavily topped pizza you would eat extracts the most from it. A plain cheese pizza under this offer is a wasted opportunity.

2. The two-item bundle

Pick any two or more qualifying items and each drops to a flat price. The workhorse of the industry and the most flexible offer on any menu.

The trick: the qualifying list usually includes sides, pasta and sandwiches, not just pizza. The best value picks are the items with the highest normal menu price relative to what the store spends making them — cheesy bread rather than plain breadsticks, a two-topping pizza rather than a plain one.

3. The family or party pack

Multiple pizzas plus sides plus a drink at a single price. Lowest cost per head of any offer, provided you genuinely have the heads.

The trick: check whether specialty pizzas carry a surcharge inside the bundle. They usually do, at a dollar or two each, which is easy to miss when you are choosing four pizzas at once.

4. Percentage off menu-price items

Typically twenty to twenty-five percent off, often described as an online-only or app-only discount.

The trick: this is the only structure that gets better the larger your order. On a small order a flat bundle wins comfortably; somewhere around a forty or fifty dollar basket the percentage starts to pull ahead. It is also the only offer that applies to items usually excluded from bundles.

5. Loyalty redemptions

Points accumulated over previous orders redeemed for a free item.

The trick: points attach to your account, not your basket, so this is the one offer that stacks with everything else. Redeem a free pizza inside a bundle order and you have effectively combined two discounts.

How to spot a deal that is worse than it looks

Four warning signs, in rough order of how often they catch people out.

The qualifying item list is narrow. A bundle that only accepts two-topping pizzas and plain breadsticks is a much smaller discount than one that accepts anything. Read the list before the headline number.

Specialty items carry a surcharge inside it. Common on family packs. Four pizzas with a dollar-fifty surcharge each is six dollars off the advertised saving.

It is delivery-only, and the fee is not included. A ten-dollar large pizza delivered is not a ten-dollar large pizza. Compare the total at checkout, not the tile price.

It requires a minimum you would not otherwise hit. Spending eight extra dollars to unlock a five-dollar discount is not a saving, however it is presented.

The comparison that actually matters

Price per square inch, not price per pizza. A large fourteen-inch pizza has roughly sixty percent more area than a twelve-inch medium, but rarely costs sixty percent more. This is why size-up offers consistently beat quantity offers, and why two-mediums-for-the-price-of-a-large sounds better than it is.

Work it out once for your local store's prices and you will not need to do it again — the ratios stay stable even as the absolute prices move.

Deals that are almost always worth taking

  • Flat carryout on one pizza, if you are collecting. Nothing beats it per item.
  • Family bundles for four or more people. Lowest cost per head, reliably.
  • Any offer that includes a drink at no extra charge. Drinks are the highest-markup line on the menu; getting them free is a genuine saving rather than a nominal one.
  • Loyalty redemptions on top of another deal. The only reliable stacking available.

Deals to be sceptical about

  • Anything requiring a spend you had not planned.
  • Percentage discounts on small orders. A flat bundle beats them below roughly thirty dollars.
  • Deals excluding the items you actually want. A discount on food you would not have ordered is not a discount.

The one habit worth building

Build your basket, note the total, then rebuild it under a different offer structure and note that total. It takes ninety seconds and finds four or five dollars often enough to be worth the ninety seconds every time.

Everything else on this page is detail. That habit is the actual advice.

title: Pizza Coupon Codes Explained: Why Yours Did Not Work
excerpt: Codes fail for four predictable reasons. Understanding how chain promotion systems are built explains all of them, and prevents most.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Photo of friends checking pizza deals on a phone at the table, for a guide explaining pizza coupon codes

faqs.question: Why does my pizza coupon code say invalid?
faqs.answer: The four common causes are that your store is not participating, your basket does not meet the qualifying item requirements, the offer has expired, or you are in delivery mode for a carryout-only offer. Store participation is the one people check last and it is the most frequent culprit.

faqs.question: Are typed coupon codes being phased out?
faqs.answer: Largely replaced by deal tiles that apply automatically when your basket qualifies. Codes still exist for targeted and partnership promotions, but the everyday discounts have moved into the ordering interface itself.

faqs.question: Where do the codes on coupon aggregator sites come from?
faqs.answer: Mostly from expired national promotions and targeted offers that were never meant to be public. Hit rates on those sites are low, which is why checking your own store's deals page is a better use of thirty seconds.

content:
A coupon code is a key. Your basket is a lock. When the key does not turn, it is almost always because the lock is a different shape than you assumed — and the shape is set at store level, which is the part nobody explains.

How chain promotion systems actually work

National chains are mostly franchise networks. Head office designs promotions and sets the terms; individual franchisees decide whether to participate, because they absorb the margin cost of the discount in their own store.

That single fact explains most coupon failures. A promotion advertised nationally is not automatically live at your store. It is live at stores that opted in. The advert is national; the offer is local.

Layered on top of that is the ordering system, which validates a code against three things: whether this store participates, whether your basket contains the qualifying items, and whether the offer is inside its date and time window. Fail any one and you get the same unhelpful message.

The four reasons codes fail

1. Your store is not participating

The most common cause and the least visible. There is no way to tell from the advert. The practical test is to look at your own store's deals page after entering your address — if the offer is not listed there, your store is not running it, and no amount of retyping will change that.

2. Your basket does not qualify

Offers specify qualifying items with more precision than the headline suggests. A two-item bundle may require two medium pizzas, not any two items. A percentage discount may exclude items already on promotion.

The tell here is that the code is accepted but the discount is smaller than expected, or the code is rejected with a message about eligible items. Swap one item and try again.

3. The offer has expired

Codes circulate on aggregator sites long after they stop working. Most of what you find by searching for a promo code is an expired national offer that someone posted eighteen months ago and never removed.

4. You are in the wrong order mode

Carryout-only offers do not appear or apply while the site has you in delivery mode, and vice versa. Because most sites default to delivery, this catches a lot of people trying to use a collection deal.

Set the order type first, before you build the basket. Switching afterwards sometimes clears the basket and always re-prices it.

Why codes are disappearing

Chains have largely moved from typed codes to deal tiles — a list of current offers, personalised to your store, that apply automatically when your basket qualifies.

From the chain's perspective this is better in every way: no expired codes leaking value, no aggregator sites distributing offers to people who would have paid full price, and complete control over what each store shows. From your perspective it is also better, because the offers you see are ones that will definitely work at your store.

Codes still exist for targeted promotions, email campaigns and partnership offers. But if you are hunting for a code on a search engine, you are looking in the place where the value has already left.

Where the discounts actually are now

  • Your store's deals page. Enter your address first, then look. Everything listed there is guaranteed to work for you.
  • The chain's own app. App-exclusive pricing is real and is usually the best available, because the chain saves on order processing and shares some of that back.
  • Email and account notifications. Targeted offers sent to your account are usually better than public ones and always work, since they were generated for your account specifically.
  • Loyalty points. The most reliable discount of all, because it does not depend on any promotion running.

A sensible troubleshooting order

  1. Confirm your delivery or carryout mode matches the offer.
  2. Check the offer appears on your own store's deals page.
  3. Read the qualifying item list and compare it to your basket, item by item.
  4. Check the date and any time-of-day restriction.
  5. If all four pass and it still fails, call the store — franchise systems occasionally have local configuration errors that phone staff can override.

What to stop doing

Stop searching for codes on aggregator sites. The hit rate is low, the codes are mostly expired, and the thirty seconds is better spent looking at the deals page for your actual store, where every listed offer is guaranteed to apply.

The discount did not disappear. It moved into the ordering interface, which is a better place for it to be.

A note on why this changed so fast

Ten years ago, a printed coupon on the back of a supermarket receipt was a perfectly good distribution channel for a pizza discount. It was slow, it was untargeted, and crucially it was hard to leak — one coupon reached one household and expired on paper.

Digital codes broke that. A code intended for a few thousand lapsed customers gets posted publicly within hours and is then redeemed by people who were going to order anyway. From the chain's point of view that is not a discount, it is a straight margin loss, and the industry response was entirely predictable: move the offer into an interface the chain controls.

Which is why the deals page personalised to your store is now where the value sits, and why the codes floating around search results are almost uniformly dead. The offer did not get worse. It moved somewhere the chain can meter it.

What to do when nothing is running

Some weeks your store genuinely has nothing good on. It happens, particularly at smaller franchise operations in quiet trading periods. The reliable fallbacks, in order:

  • Switch to carryout. The flat carryout rate is close to a permanent fixture at most chains and rarely disappears entirely.
  • Check a second store if more than one serves your address. Participation is decided individually, so a neighbouring store may be running something yours is not.
  • Look at your points balance. A redemption does not depend on any promotion running at all, which makes it the one discount that is always available once you have earned it.
  • Shift the order to a weekday lunchtime if timing is flexible. Off-peak offers exist precisely because those hours are quiet.

None of that requires a code, which is rather the point.

title: Hand Tossed vs Thin Crust vs Pan: Which to Order?
excerpt: Crust is the only free decision on a pizza — and it changes the texture, calories, topping capacity and whether leftovers are worth keeping.
author: maha-iqbal

faqs.question: Which pizza crust has the fewest calories?
faqs.answer: Thin crust, by a clear margin — roughly a third less than hand tossed on the base alone, with toppings and cheese unchanged. Because crust choice is usually free, it is the cheapest calorie reduction available on a chain pizza.

faqs.question: Does pan pizza cost more?
faqs.answer: Usually a small upcharge over hand tossed, and that upcharge often applies on top of deal pricing rather than being absorbed into it. It is also frequently unavailable in the largest size because pans come in fixed dimensions.

faqs.question: Which crust holds the most toppings?
faqs.answer: Pan, then hand tossed, then thin. A thin crust struggles beyond two or three toppings, particularly wet vegetables, because there is not enough structure to support the weight and moisture.

content:
Crust is the most consequential decision on a chain pizza order and, at most stores, the only free one. Changing from hand tossed to thin crust costs nothing and changes the calorie count, the texture, the number of toppings the pizza can carry and how it survives until tomorrow.

Here is what each one actually is, and when to pick it.

Hand tossed: the default

A medium-thickness base with a raised outer rim, soft in the middle, chewy at the edge. This is the crust every deal assumes and every price is quoted against.

Best for: most orders. It carries three or four toppings comfortably, it survives a delivery journey, and it reheats acceptably. There is a reason it is the default.

Weaknesses: it is a compromise. It is not as crisp as thin, not as rich as pan, and it does nothing exceptionally.

Roughly: around 200 calories per slice of a large before toppings.

Thin crust: the calorie decision

Rolled rather than tossed, no raised rim, crisp rather than chewy, usually cut into squares.

Best for: anyone who wants to cut calories without changing what they eat. Roughly a third less than hand tossed on the base, with the cheese and toppings identical, and it costs nothing to switch. As a nutrition intervention this is unusually painless — nothing is removed from the pizza except dough.

Also better for anyone who dislikes the doughy centre of a chain pizza, which is a real and common complaint.

Weaknesses: it will not hold heavy toppings. Two or three is the practical limit and wet vegetables need a well-done bake. It also feeds fewer people than the same-diameter hand tossed, because there is genuinely less food, and it goes stale fastest of the three.

Roughly: around 140 calories per equivalent portion of a large before toppings.

Pan: the rich one

Baked in an oiled pan, which fries the underside as it bakes and produces a thick, golden, slightly crunchy bottom edge.

Best for: people who want the crust to be part of the meal rather than a vehicle. Also the best of the three for leftovers by some distance — the oil in the base keeps it from drying out overnight, and a reheated pan slice in a hot oven is genuinely good.

Weaknesses: it usually carries an upcharge, that upcharge is often applied on top of deal pricing, and the largest sizes may not be available because pans are physical objects in fixed dimensions. It is also the highest-calorie crust by a wide margin.

Roughly: around 280 calories per slice of a large before toppings.

The comparison in practice

Take the same large pizza with pepperoni and mushroom, and change nothing but the crust:

  • Thin: the lightest option, crisp, best eaten immediately, awkward with a third topping.
  • Hand tossed: the safe pick, holds up to delivery, reheats fine, no strong character.
  • Pan: the most substantial, the most expensive, the best tomorrow, the heaviest.

Over a whole large pizza, the gap between thin and pan is several hundred calories from a decision that takes one click and, for two of the three options, costs nothing.

How to choose, quickly

Ordering for a group? Hand tossed. It suits the widest range of preferences and holds up while people help themselves over an hour.

Watching calories? Thin crust. It is the largest free reduction available on a chain pizza and does not touch the toppings.

Want leftovers? Pan. It is the only crust that is genuinely good the following day.

Ordering four or five toppings? Pan or hand tossed. Thin will not hold them.

Using a deal? Hand tossed or thin, since pan may carry an upcharge that eats into the discount.

Free modifications worth knowing

Whatever crust you pick, these are free at most stores and change the result:

  • Well done. Extra oven time. Fixes soggy centres on vegetable-heavy pizzas and crisps up thin crust properly. Do not use it on a barbecue-sauce base, where the sugar catches.
  • Light sauce. Helps thin crust considerably if you find it goes soft.
  • Light cheese. A real calorie reduction that also lets a thin crust stay crisp.
  • Square cut. Available on any crust at most stores, not just thin. Better for sharing at a table where people are grazing.

The short answer

Hand tossed if you have no strong preference. Thin crust if calories matter, because it is the only free lever of that size. Pan if you want the crust to be the point, and if you are prepared for the upcharge.

The one thing not worth doing is defaulting without thinking about it. It is the only decision on the order that is free, reversible next time, and changes the pizza more than any single topping.

What crust does to the rest of your order

Crust choice quietly changes decisions further down the basket, and it is worth thinking one step ahead.

A large thin crust has less food on it than a large hand tossed of the same diameter, so a table that would be satisfied by one hand-tossed large may want a side alongside a thin one. That side costs money the free crust switch did not. Ordering thin crust to save calories and then adding cheesy bread to fill the gap is a net loss on both counts.

Pan works the other way. It is more filling per slice, so a pan pizza often removes the need for a side entirely — which can offset the upcharge that made it look expensive in the first place.

A practical ordering script

If you want a single default that will rarely be wrong: hand tossed, well done, one meat topping and as many vegetables as you like. That combination survives delivery, holds its toppings, suits a mixed table, is priced at the standard rate inside every deal, and lands in the middle of the calorie range without anyone having to think about it.

Deviate from that deliberately — thin when calories are the priority, pan when you want leftovers or when the crust is the point. What is not worth doing is deviating by accident, which is what happens when you click through the default without noticing there was a choice at all.

title: Large vs Medium Pizza: The Maths Nobody Does at Checkout
excerpt: A large pizza is not a slightly bigger medium. It is roughly sixty percent more pizza, and it almost never costs sixty percent more.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Photo comparing large and medium pizza value
keywords: how many people does a large pizza feed

pricing.label: Typical size ladder, one-topping pizza
pricing.note: Medium through extra-large at menu price. The area increases faster than the price does at every step.

faqs.question: Is a large pizza better value than a medium?
faqs.answer: Almost always. A fourteen-inch large has roughly sixty percent more area than a twelve-inch medium but typically costs only twenty-five to thirty percent more, which makes the price per square inch meaningfully lower.

faqs.question: Are two mediums better than one large?
faqs.answer: Two twelve-inch mediums give more total area than one fourteen-inch large, so if a deal prices two mediums near the price of one large, the mediums win on quantity. At standard menu prices, one large wins on price per square inch.

faqs.question: How many people does a large pizza feed?
faqs.answer: Two to three adults as a meal, or four with sides on the table. A large cut into eight slices gives three people two to three slices each, which is where most people naturally stop.

content:
Pizza is sold by diameter and eaten by area, and those two things do not scale together. That single mismatch is responsible for most of the money people leave on the table when they order.

A twelve-inch medium has about 113 square inches of pizza. A fourteen-inch large has about 154. That is roughly sixty percent more food for two extra inches of width — and at almost every chain, that sixty percent more food costs about twenty-five to thirty percent more money.

The size ladder, worked through

Using representative menu prices for a one-topping pizza:

SizeDiameterApprox. areaExample pricePrice per sq inch
Small10 in79 sq in$10.4913.3¢
Medium12 in113 sq in$13.4911.9¢
Large14 in154 sq in$16.4910.7¢
Extra Large16 in201 sq in$18.999.4¢

The pattern is consistent and it goes one way: every step up the ladder lowers the price per square inch. Going from small to extra-large cuts the unit cost of pizza by almost thirty percent.

The small pizza is, by this measure, the worst value item on any chain menu. It exists for people ordering alone who do not want leftovers, which is a legitimate reason to buy it — but it is not a cheap pizza, it is a small one.

Where the intuition goes wrong

People compare pizzas by diameter because that is the number on the menu. Two inches sounds like a small difference. But area scales with the square of the radius, so two inches of diameter on a twelve-inch pizza is a much bigger jump than the number implies.

Put concretely: nobody would describe a large as sixty percent more pizza than a medium, but that is what it is.

The two-mediums question

This comes up constantly, usually because a deal prices two mediums attractively.

Two twelve-inch mediums give 226 square inches. One fourteen-inch large gives 154. So two mediums are roughly forty-five percent more pizza than one large — meaningfully more food, and if a bundle prices them close to a single large, the mediums are clearly the better buy.

At standard menu prices, though, two mediums cost far more than one large while a single large costs less per square inch. The deal is what flips it, not the sizes themselves.

The useful rule: if you need more pizza, size up first and add a second pizza only when you have run out of sizes. Going medium to large costs a few dollars; adding a second medium costs a whole pizza.

When a smaller pizza is the right answer

Value per square inch is not the only consideration.

  • Two people with different tastes. Two smalls with different toppings can beat one large that half the table only tolerates. Though a half-and-half large is usually cheaper still.
  • Pan crust. Often unavailable in extra-large because pans come in fixed sizes, so the ladder stops early.
  • Thin crust. There is less food on the same diameter, so a large thin crust feeds fewer people than a large hand tossed. Size up accordingly.
  • You genuinely will not eat it. Cheap pizza in the bin is not cheap. Thin crust in particular is poor the next day.

How much does each size actually feed?

Working from typical appetites rather than official portion guidance:

  • Small (10 in): one adult, comfortably.
  • Medium (12 in): two adults, or one with leftovers.
  • Large (14 in): two to three adults, or four with sides on the table.
  • Extra-large (16 in): three to four adults, or five with sides.

The reliable planning number is two to three slices per adult when there are sides, three to four when the pizza is the whole meal.

What to do with this

Three practical takeaways.

Size up before you add. The step up the ladder is always cheaper per unit of pizza than a whole additional pizza.

Work out your store's price per square inch once. The absolute prices move; the ratios stay stable. One calculation tells you where the value sits for years.

Ignore the diameter, think about the area. Two inches is not a small difference. It is the difference between feeding two people and feeding three.

Why chains price it this way

It is tempting to read the size ladder as generosity. It is not — it is cost structure.

The expensive parts of making a pizza barely change with size. Someone still takes the order, stretches a base, applies sauce and cheese, runs it through an oven and boxes it. The additional cost of a fourteen-inch pizza over a twelve-inch one is a modest amount of dough, sauce, cheese and a marginally larger box.

So the store can charge twenty-five percent more for sixty percent more pizza and still improve its margin on the transaction. Sizing up is a rare case where what is good for you and what is good for them point the same direction, which is exactly why the option is offered so prominently at checkout.

The one place the maths stops working

Everything above assumes you eat the pizza. Cheap pizza in the bin is not cheap, and the calculation reverses completely on any pizza that reheats badly.

Thin crust is the clearest case: it stales fastest of any base and a large thin crust bought for a household of two is often a large thin crust with a third of it wasted. Pan is the opposite — it is genuinely good the next day, so sizing up carries less risk.

The honest rule is to size up to the largest pizza your household will finish across two sittings, and to weight that judgement by which crust you have chosen. That is a slightly less satisfying answer than always order the extra-large, but it is the one that survives contact with a real fridge.

title: Pizza Rewards Programmes: What the Points Are Worth
excerpt: Most pizza loyalty schemes count orders, not dollars. That one design choice changes the optimal way to use them completely.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Photo for a guide to pizza rewards programmes

faqs.question: Do pizza rewards points depend on how much I spend?
faqs.answer: At most pizza chains, no. Points are awarded per qualifying order above a small minimum, so a fifteen-dollar order and a sixty-dollar order typically earn the same. That makes frequent small orders far more efficient than occasional large ones.

faqs.question: Do carryout orders earn points?
faqs.answer: Yes at most chains, at the same rate as delivery. People routinely assume otherwise and lose points on exactly the orders they should be placing, since carryout is also the cheapest way to order.

faqs.question: Do loyalty points expire?
faqs.answer: Commonly after a period of account inactivity rather than on a fixed date from when they were earned. A single qualifying order usually resets the clock on your whole balance.

content:
Pizza loyalty schemes are unusual, and the way they are unusual is worth understanding because it inverts the normal logic of rewards programmes.

Most loyalty schemes — airlines, supermarkets, credit cards — award points in proportion to spending. Spend twice as much, earn twice as much. Pizza chains generally do not work that way. They award points per order above a modest minimum, which means a fifteen-dollar order and a sixty-dollar order earn the same points.

Everything useful about optimising these programmes follows from that one design choice.

The basic structure

Typical shape across the major chains: you earn a fixed number of points for each qualifying order over a minimum spend, and at a threshold — commonly around sixty points, reached in six orders — you can redeem for a free pizza, usually a medium with a limited number of toppings.

Points sit on your account rather than on your basket, which has one important consequence: redemptions generally stack with other offers. It is the only reliable stacking available in chain pizza.

What the points are actually worth

If six qualifying orders earn a free medium pizza with a menu price around thirteen dollars, each order is generating roughly two dollars of value.

On a fifteen-dollar minimum order, that is an effective discount of about thirteen percent. On a sixty-dollar family order, the same two dollars is about three percent.

The programme rewards frequency, not spending. That is the whole insight.

How to actually optimise it

Split large orders when you can

If you were going to place a sixty-dollar order and could reasonably split it into two thirty-dollar orders on different days, you earn twice the points for the same total spend. Not always practical, but worth knowing that the option exists.

Never check out as a guest

Points do not attach to guest orders and most schemes will not add them retrospectively. Every guest checkout is roughly two dollars thrown away.

Remember carryout earns too

At most chains carryout orders earn at the same rate as delivery. Since carryout is also the cheapest way to order, this is the single best combination available — lowest price and full points on the same transaction.

Redeem on top of a deal, not instead of one

Because the redemption comes off your account rather than out of the basket, you can generally use a free-pizza redemption inside an order that is already on a bundle price. Redeeming on a full-price order wastes the stacking.

Redeem for the most expensive qualifying item

If the redemption is any medium pizza, take a specialty one rather than a plain cheese. Same points, more pizza.

The parts that cost people points

The order minimum. There is usually a spend threshold below which an order earns nothing. A single side does not qualify. Check the figure for your chain — an order a dollar under the line earns exactly zero.

Expiry through inactivity. Points commonly lapse after a period without any qualifying order, rather than expiring individually. One order resets the clock on the whole balance, which means an occasional order protects a balance you have already built.

Multiple accounts. Two people in a household ordering under separate accounts earn at half the rate of one shared account. Consolidate.

Third-party delivery apps. Orders placed through an aggregator generally do not earn chain loyalty points, because the transaction never touches the chain's own account system. That is a real hidden cost of ordering through those platforms, on top of their markup.

Are they worth joining?

Yes, with a caveat. Signing up costs nothing and the effective discount for a regular orderer is meaningful — around ten percent for someone who orders modest amounts frequently.

The caveat is behavioural. These schemes are designed to increase order frequency, and they work. If the existence of a points balance is nudging you into ordering pizza more often than you otherwise would, the programme is making money from you rather than the other way round. That is not a reason to avoid it; it is a reason to be honest about which is happening.

The short version

  • Points usually track orders, not spending — frequency beats size.
  • Always sign in. Guest checkouts earn nothing.
  • Carryout earns too, and is also the cheapest way to order.
  • Redeem alongside a deal, not instead of one.
  • Watch the minimum spend and the inactivity clock.

How this compares to other loyalty schemes

It is worth putting pizza rewards next to the schemes people are more used to, because the mental model transfers badly.

An airline programme rewards spending: a business-class fare earns many times what an economy fare does, and the scheme is explicitly designed to make high spenders more loyal. A supermarket scheme is usually a straightforward percentage back, so the behaviour it rewards is simply shopping there.

A pizza scheme that counts orders rewards neither. It rewards habit — the behaviour of choosing this chain rather than the one down the road, repeatedly, regardless of how much you spend when you do. That is a different product, aimed at a different problem, and it is why the optimisation advice is inverted from what you would apply to an airline card.

Whether to chase a threshold

One question we get regularly: if you are one order away from a free pizza, is it worth placing an order you did not want?

Almost never. A qualifying order typically costs fifteen dollars or more to earn roughly two dollars of value. Spending fifteen to unlock the last two is a poor trade unless you were going to order that week anyway.

Where it does make sense is timing rather than volume. If you were going to order at some point in the next fortnight and your points are approaching an inactivity expiry, bringing that order forward protects a balance you have already earned. That is not chasing a threshold; it is not throwing away work you have already done.

title: How to Order Pizza Online Without Overpaying
excerpt: The order in which you click things changes what you pay. Here is the sequence that consistently produces the lowest total.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Photo for a step-by-step online pizza ordering guide

faqs.question: Should I choose delivery or carryout first?
faqs.answer: First, before anything else. Carryout-only pricing does not appear while the site has you in delivery mode, and switching later re-prices the basket or clears it entirely at some chains.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to order on the app than the website?
faqs.answer: Often marginally, because app-exclusive offers are common and processing an app order costs the chain less. The difference is usually small but it is real, and it is worth checking both before a large order.

faqs.question: Should I order through a third-party delivery app?
faqs.answer: Generally not, if the chain delivers to you directly. Aggregator platforms typically carry marked-up menu prices plus their own service fees, and orders placed through them usually do not earn chain loyalty points.

content:
Two people can order the same food from the same store on the same evening and pay eight dollars differently. The food is identical. What differs is the sequence of decisions.

Here is the sequence that works, with the reasoning for each step.

Step 1: Choose the chain's own channel

Order from the chain's site or app, not a third-party delivery platform, if the chain delivers to your address directly.

Aggregator platforms typically list marked-up menu prices, add their own service fees, and — importantly — orders placed through them usually do not earn chain loyalty points. On a thirty-dollar order the combined difference is frequently six to eight dollars.

Between the chain's own website and its app, the app is usually marginally cheaper because app-exclusive offers are common. Not always worth installing an app for one order; worth it if you order monthly.

Step 2: Set the order type before anything else

Delivery or carryout, chosen first.

This matters more than it sounds. Carryout-only offers do not display while the site has you in delivery mode. If you build a basket in delivery mode and switch afterwards, some chains re-price everything and others clear the basket entirely.

Step 3: Enter your address and confirm your store

Store assignment determines which offers you see, because franchisees opt into promotions individually. Two stores four miles apart can show different deals.

If more than one store serves your address, it is worth checking both. This is uncommon in dense cities and quite common in suburban areas.

Step 4: Sign in before you build the basket

Points do not attach to guest orders. Signing in halfway through checkout occasionally clears the basket and sometimes loses an applied offer.

Sign in first, every time. It takes ten seconds and it is the most commonly skipped step on this list.

Step 5: Read the deals page before the menu

This is the step that separates a cheap order from an expensive one.

Look at the current offers first, then decide what to order. Most people do it the other way round — build what they want from the menu, then look for a discount that fits — and end up with a basket that qualifies for nothing.

Starting from the deals page means you are choosing between structures rather than trying to retrofit a discount onto a basket.

Step 6: Build from inside the deal tile

If you are using an offer, click into the deal and build the pizza there rather than adding items from the main menu and hoping the discount catches.

Building from the menu frequently applies per-topping charges that the deal would have covered. It is the most common way people lose money that they had a coupon for.

Step 7: Put the most expensive qualifying item into the deal slot

A flat rate buys a plain cheese pizza or a fully loaded one for the same money. Choose deliberately.

Same for a two-item bundle: cheesy bread rather than plain breadsticks, a specialty pizza rather than a one-topping, wherever the flat price covers both.

Step 8: Apply the free modifications

Light or extra sauce, light cheese, well-done bake, square cut. All free at most stores, all change the pizza. Extra cheese and extra meat are paid.

Well done is the single most useful one — it fixes soggy centres on vegetable-heavy pizzas. Skip it on a barbecue-sauce base, where the sugar catches at the edges.

Step 9: Price the basket a second way

Before checking out, rebuild the same food under a different offer structure and compare totals.

A percentage discount on menu prices beats a flat bundle above roughly thirty or forty dollars. Below that, the bundle wins. Ninety seconds, four or five dollars, often enough to be worth doing every time.

Step 10: Write proper delivery instructions

Gate code, buzzer number, apartment number, which entrance, anything unusual about the building.

Ask any delivery driver and they'll say the same thing: the last fifty feet is where deliveries go wrong, not the drive. A driver with your gate code in the notes field does not need to call you from a spot where they have no signal.

Step 11: Check the total, not the tile price

The advertised price on a deal tile is the food. The total includes tax, delivery fee, any small-order surcharge and the tip. Look at the final number before confirming — that is the one you are actually paying.

The compressed version

  1. Chain's own app or site.
  2. Order type first.
  3. Confirm the store.
  4. Sign in.
  5. Deals page before the menu.
  6. Build inside the deal.
  7. Most expensive qualifying item in the slot.
  8. Free modifications.
  9. Price it a second way.
  10. Real delivery instructions.
  11. Check the total.

It sounds like a lot written out. In practice it is about two minutes and it is the difference between the top and bottom of an eight-dollar range on the same food.

title: The Delivery Fee Is Not a Tip: Where It Goes
excerpt: A former driver explains what the delivery fee covers, what drivers are actually paid, and why the two are constantly confused at checkout.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Photo explaining pizza delivery fees and driver tips
keywords: does delivery fee go to driver

faqs.question: Does the pizza delivery fee go to the driver?
faqs.answer: At most chains, no. It is a store charge covering insurance, vehicle costs and operational overhead. Drivers are typically paid an hourly wage plus tips, sometimes with a small per-run reimbursement that does not resemble the fee amount.

faqs.question: How much should I tip a pizza delivery driver?
faqs.answer: A common benchmark is fifteen to twenty percent of the food total, with a floor of three to five dollars on small orders, and more in bad weather or for a difficult delivery. Percentage alone breaks down on very small orders because the driving effort is the same regardless of order size.

faqs.question: Is it better to tip in cash or on the card?
faqs.answer: Either reaches the driver at most chains, but cash reaches them the same night rather than in a future payslip. Card tips are reliable at chain stores; cash is simply faster.

content:
The single most common misunderstanding among people ordering delivery — and it comes up constantly, in doorways, on the phone, in the notes people leave on orders — is that the delivery fee is the driver's payment.

It is not. Here is what is actually going on, and why the checkout screen makes it so easy to get wrong.

What the delivery fee covers

The delivery fee is a store charge. At most chains it goes to the store's operating account and covers the costs of running a delivery operation: commercial insurance, wear on company vehicles where those are used, the additional staffing that dispatch requires, and general overhead.

It is not a driver payment, it is not distributed as one, and it is not calculated as one. Its size relates to what delivery costs the store, not to what any individual driver did.

What drivers are actually paid

Typical structure at a chain store:

  • An hourly wage, which in many jurisdictions is a tipped wage below the standard minimum, topped up to the minimum if tips fall short.
  • Tips, which make up the majority of take-home pay on a good shift.
  • Sometimes a small per-delivery reimbursement toward fuel and vehicle costs when the driver uses their own car. This is usually a fraction of the delivery fee.

The practical consequence: on a slow night, a driver's income is close to the wage floor. On a busy night it is mostly tips. The delivery fee does not move with either.

Why the confusion is so persistent

Because the checkout screen puts them next to each other.

You see a line for a delivery fee and a line for a tip, adjacent, both framed as the cost of having food brought to you. It is entirely reasonable to read that as being asked to pay twice for the same service. Nothing on the screen explains that one goes to the store and the other goes to the person driving.

I do not think this is deliberate deception. I do think it is a design that has been left alone because clarifying it would probably reduce fee revenue, tip amounts, or both.

What this means for what you should pay

The uncomfortable version: if you reduce the tip because a delivery fee was already charged, the person absorbing that reduction is the driver. The chain's revenue is unaffected.

Rough benchmarks I would stand behind:

  • Fifteen to twenty percent of the food total as a baseline, as you would in a restaurant.
  • A floor of three to five dollars regardless of order size. A ten-dollar order takes the same drive as a forty-dollar one; percentage alone under-pays on small orders.
  • More in bad weather. Snow, ice and heavy rain make the job genuinely harder and slower, and slower means fewer runs per shift, which means less income across the whole night.
  • More for difficulty. Fourth-floor walk-up, gated complex, long driveway, unclear address — all of it costs the driver time that they are not otherwise compensated for.

Cash or card?

At a chain store, card tips reach the driver. This is worth saying clearly because a persistent rumour claims otherwise, and it costs drivers money.

The genuine difference is timing. Cash is in the driver's pocket that night. A card tip usually arrives in a future payslip. Both reach them; one reaches them faster.

If your budget is tight

There are better places to cut than the tip, and I would rank them roughly like this:

  1. Drop the drinks. Roughly double supermarket price, and no food is lost.
  2. Switch to carryout if the store is close. No delivery, no fee, no tip owed, and usually a cheaper pizza price.
  3. Order from a bundle rather than the menu.
  4. Skip the paid extras — extra cheese, extra meat.

All four save more than trimming a tip does, and none of them come out of anyone's wages.

The one-line summary

The fee is the store's. The tip is the driver's. They are next to each other on the screen because of how checkout pages are laid out, not because they are two halves of the same payment.

What a shift actually looks like

Some context for why the tip matters as much as it does.

A driver's income is essentially tips per hour. Everything that reduces how many deliveries fit into an hour reduces income for the whole shift, not just for the delivery that was slow. A single long run to the edge of the zone can cost two shorter runs. A gated complex where nobody answers the callbox can cost ten minutes and the run behind it.

That is why weather tipping is not sentimentality. In snow, a driver might complete two-thirds of their normal runs while taking on considerably more risk. The hourly income falls at exactly the moment the job gets harder, and the only thing that offsets it is what people at the door decide to do.

Where the fee actually goes, in slightly more detail

Commercial insurance is the largest single component at most stores, and it is genuinely expensive — insuring a fleet of drivers making frequent short trips in all weather is not a cheap product. Beyond that the fee covers vehicle maintenance where the store owns cars, the additional staffing that dispatch requires, and general operating overhead.

Some stores do pay drivers a small per-delivery reimbursement toward fuel and wear when the driver uses their own car. It is usually a fraction of the fee, it is intended to cover costs rather than to compensate labour, and it is not a tip by any reasonable definition.

None of this makes the fee unreasonable. Delivery does cost the store money. It just is not the driver's money, and the checkout screen does nothing to tell you that.

title: The Mix and Match Deal, Explained Properly
excerpt: The two-items-for-a-flat-price offer is the most flexible deal in chain pizza and the easiest to use badly. Here is how to extract the most from it.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Photo explaining the mix and match pizza deal

faqs.question: What counts as a qualifying item in a mix and match deal?
faqs.answer: Typically medium two-topping pizzas, bread sides, baked pasta, sandwiches, boneless chicken and desserts, though the exact list varies by chain and by store. Wings, specialty pizzas and drinks are the most commonly excluded or surcharged items.

faqs.question: Which items give the best value in a mix and match?
faqs.answer: The items with the highest standalone menu price relative to what the store spends producing them — cheesy bread over plain breadsticks, a fully topped pizza over a plain one, baked pasta over a dessert.

faqs.question: Can I order more than two items on a mix and match deal?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and the flat rate applies to each additional qualifying item. For groups this is often better value than a fixed family bundle, because you control exactly what goes in.

content:
The mix and match — pick any two or more qualifying items, each at one flat price — is the most-used deal structure in chain pizza, and the one where the gap between using it well and using it badly is widest.

Two people can order the same number of items under the same offer and one of them can walk away with substantially more food. Here is how that happens.

How the offer is constructed

The chain defines a list of qualifying items and a single price that applies to any of them. From your side that looks like a discount. From the store's side it is a weighted average: some items on that list cost far less to produce than others, and the flat price is set knowing roughly how often each gets chosen.

Which means the offer is priced around the typical selection. Choose atypically and you come out ahead.

Rule one: pick the items with the highest standalone price

If a two-item bundle prices any qualifying item at seven dollars, and breadsticks normally cost six-fifty while cheesy bread costs eight-fifty, the cheesy bread extracts two dollars more from the same slot.

Applied across a whole basket:

  • Cheesy bread over plain breadsticks.
  • A two-topping pizza over a plain cheese one, where the deal allows two toppings.
  • Baked pasta or a sandwich over a dessert, since desserts usually carry the lowest standalone price on the list.
  • Boneless chicken over wings, where both qualify — more meat per dollar, since there is no bone weight.

Rule two: check what is excluded before you plan the order

The exclusions are where these offers quietly get worse:

Specialty pizzas frequently carry a surcharge inside the bundle, typically a dollar or two. Not disqualifying, but it changes the maths on a four-pizza order.

Wings are often excluded entirely or surcharged, because they are among the most expensive items for the store to serve.

Drinks almost never qualify. They may count toward a delivery minimum but not as a bundle item.

Crust upgrades — pan in particular — often carry an upcharge on top of the deal price.

Rule three: use more than two slots when it suits you

Most mix and match offers do not stop at two. The flat rate applies to each additional qualifying item, which makes this structure genuinely competitive with a fixed family pack for a group.

The advantage over a family bundle is control. A family pack dictates the composition — two pizzas, one side, one drink — whereas four mix and match slots can be four pizzas, or two pizzas and two pastas, or whatever the table actually wants.

Price both. For four or more items they land close together often enough that it is worth thirty seconds.

Rule four: this is where a two-medium order makes sense

At standard menu prices, one large pizza is better value per square inch than two mediums. Under a flat-rate mix and match, that reverses: two mediums at a flat rate each give roughly forty-five percent more total pizza than a single large, for a predictable price.

This is the specific situation where the usual size-up advice does not apply, and it is worth knowing which situation you are in.

Rule five: watch what happens to the total

Two items at seven dollars is fourteen dollars of food, before tax, delivery fee and tip. On a delivery order that fourteen can become twenty-two by the time you confirm.

The deal is real; the tile price is not the total. This is not specific to mix and match, but the flat per-item framing makes it especially easy to under-estimate where you will land.

A worked example

Same offer, two ways of using it. Three items at a flat seven dollars each, twenty-one dollars either way:

Used carelessly: a plain cheese medium, plain breadsticks, and a dessert. Standalone menu value around twenty-six dollars.

Used deliberately: a two-topping medium, cheesy bread, and a baked pasta. Standalone menu value around thirty-four dollars.

Same price, same number of items, eight dollars of difference. That is the entire skill involved.

The summary

  • Fill each slot with the highest standalone-price qualifying item you will actually eat.
  • Check the exclusion and surcharge list before planning.
  • Use extra slots for a group rather than defaulting to a fixed family pack.
  • Two mediums beat one large under a flat rate, unlike at menu prices.
  • Judge the deal on the checkout total, not the tile.

Why chains keep this offer running

The mix and match survives every promotional refresh because it solves a problem specific to pizza economics: the store wants your basket to contain more than one item.

A single-pizza order and a three-item order consume almost the same fixed costs — the same order handling, the same oven cycle window, the same delivery run. The marginal cost of adding breadsticks to a bag that is already going out is very small. So an offer that pushes a one-item basket to a three-item basket improves the store's return on that delivery substantially, even at a discounted price per item.

Which is why the flat rate is often surprisingly good. The chain is not being generous; it is buying basket size, and basket size is worth more to it than the margin it gave up.

Ordering for one person

The obvious objection to a multi-item deal is that you are one person and do not want three items.

Two things worth knowing. First, the qualifying list usually includes items that keep well — boneless chicken reheats better than almost anything on the menu, and pan crust is genuinely good the next day. A two-item deal for one person is frequently two meals rather than one oversized one.

Second, if it genuinely is not worth it, the flat carryout offer on a single pizza exists precisely for this case and beats the bundle comfortably at one item. The mistake is assuming the promoted deal is the right deal for your order — it is the right deal for the average order, which is not the same thing.

title: Which Pizza Toppings Are Worth Paying For?
excerpt: Every topping costs the same at checkout and they are emphatically not worth the same. A ranking based on what you actually get.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Photo ranking pizza toppings by value

faqs.question: Do all pizza toppings cost the same?
faqs.answer: At most chains, yes — a flat per-topping charge that scales with pizza size, regardless of whether you choose mushrooms or bacon. Since the charge is uniform but the value clearly is not, meat toppings extract more from each charge than vegetables do.

faqs.question: Is extra cheese worth the money?
faqs.answer: Rarely, as a paid modification. It is one of the more expensive add-ons and the difference is often barely visible on a well-made pizza. A specialty pizza inside a deal usually delivers more for the same money.

faqs.question: How many toppings before a specialty pizza is cheaper?
faqs.answer: Usually three or four on a large, depending on your store's per-topping rate. Past that point a specialty pizza carrying five or six toppings is frequently cheaper than a custom one carrying four.

content:
Chain pizza toppings are priced as a single flat charge per topping, scaled by pizza size. Mushrooms cost what bacon costs. Onions cost what sausage costs.

That uniform pricing is convenient for the store and slightly absurd for you, because the ingredients differ enormously in what they cost to buy, how much of them arrives on the pizza, and how much they change the eating experience.

Here is a ranking, and the reasoning behind it.

The best value toppings

1. Pepperoni

The most-ordered topping in the country for a reason. It arrives in genuine quantity, it changes the flavour of the whole pizza, and it is the topping most likely to be included free inside a deal because offers are modelled around it.

2. Italian sausage

Applied in substantial pieces, high in flavour, and it renders fat into the cheese during the bake, which spreads the effect across the whole slice rather than concentrating it where the pieces sit.

3. Bacon

Strong flavour per gram, so even a modest quantity registers. It also crisps in the oven, adding texture that most toppings do not.

4. Extra pepperoni on an existing pepperoni pizza

Unusual entry, but sound: it is the one paid modification where the change is unambiguous. You can see it and taste it.

Middling value

5. Grilled chicken

Decent quantity and genuine protein, but mild — it needs a sauce that carries it, which is why chicken appears on barbecue and buffalo bases rather than plain tomato.

6. Mushrooms

Applied generously and they do change the character of a pizza. But they release water during the bake and can soften the base, particularly on thin crust. Order well done if you use them.

7. Black olives

Assertive flavour, so a small quantity does work. Genuinely divisive though, which limits their usefulness on a shared pizza.

Poor value

8. Onions

Cheap to buy, applied in moderate quantity, and they largely melt into the background during the bake. Perfectly nice; barely detectable as a paid addition.

9. Green peppers

Similar problem, plus a high water content that works against the base. On a heavily topped pizza you will struggle to identify them at all.

10. Diced tomato

Adding tomato to a tomato-sauce base. The pizza is already tomato-flavoured, and fresh tomato mostly adds moisture.

11. Extra cheese

Consistently the weakest paid modification. It is one of the more expensive add-ons and, on a pizza that already carries a full cheese covering, the difference is frequently invisible. If you want a richer pizza, a meat topping does more for the same money.

The rule that matters more than the ranking

Count your toppings before you check out.

Because each topping carries a flat charge that scales with size, a build-your-own with four toppings on a large routinely costs more than a specialty pizza carrying five or six. The specialty section is a pre-bundled topping discount, and past three toppings it usually wins.

This is the single most common way people overspend on chain pizza, and it takes thirty seconds to check.

The free modifications, which are underused

None of these cost anything at most stores and all of them change the pizza more than a fourth topping would:

  • Well done. Fixes the soggy centre that vegetables cause. Avoid on a barbecue base, where the sugar catches.
  • Light sauce. Helps thin crust stay crisp.
  • Extra sauce. Costs nothing and changes the balance of the pizza noticeably.
  • Light cheese. A genuine calorie reduction that also lets the toppings come through.
  • Removing a topping from a specialty pizza. Free, where adding one is not. Subtracting is the cheap way to customise.

A note on nutrition

Since I edit the nutrition side of this site, the honest note: vegetable toppings add very little to the calorie count and meat toppings add meaningfully — roughly thirty to forty calories per slice for a meat topping against ten or so for a vegetable.

So the value ranking and the nutrition ranking point in opposite directions, which is entirely predictable. If calories are the priority, the crust choice is a much bigger lever than the toppings: switching to thin crust saves more than removing every meat topping would.

The short version

Meats extract the most from a flat per-topping charge. Vegetables mostly do not. Extra cheese is the weakest paid add-on on the board. And past three toppings, check the specialty menu before you pay for a fourth.

Why the flat per-topping charge exists

Charging the same for mushrooms and bacon is obviously not cost-based. It is interface-based.

A build-your-own ordering flow with per-ingredient pricing would require the customer to evaluate thirty prices while assembling a pizza, and every additional decision at that point in the flow loses orders. One number that applies to everything is faster to understand, faster to click through and much easier to describe in a deal.

So the store prices toppings as an average and accepts that some customers extract more from the charge than others. Being one of the customers who extracts more costs nothing except knowing which is which.

Half-and-half, the underused option

One structural point that beats any individual topping choice: at most chains a half-and-half pizza costs the price of the more expensive half rather than carrying a premium.

That has a genuinely useful consequence. Two half-and-half larges cover four different topping combinations at the price of two pizzas, which is almost always better for a mixed table than buying four smalls or ordering one supreme that half the table tolerates rather than enjoys.

It also lets you put an expensive specialty on one half and something plain on the other without paying the full specialty price twice. For a household where one person wants a loaded meat pizza and another wants cheese, this is the single most useful thing on this page.

title: Gluten-Free Pizza at Chains: What to Know First
excerpt: A gluten-free crust is not the same as a gluten-free kitchen. What that distinction means depends entirely on why you are avoiding gluten.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Photo for a guide to gluten-free pizza options

faqs.question: Is chain gluten-free pizza safe for coeliac disease?
faqs.answer: Most chains explicitly state it is not, because the crust is prepared in a kitchen where wheat flour is airborne and shared surfaces and utensils are used. The crust itself is made without gluten ingredients; the environment is not gluten-free, and chains are generally clear about this distinction.

faqs.question: Does gluten-free crust cost more?
faqs.answer: Usually a few dollars more than a standard base, and it is commonly excluded from deal pricing or carries an upcharge inside it. It is also typically only available in one size, most often a small or medium.

faqs.question: Which pizza toppings contain gluten?
faqs.answer: Most standard toppings do not, but seasoned meats and sauces are the ones to check — some contain wheat-based binders or thickeners. Request current allergen information from the chain rather than assuming, since suppliers and recipes change.

content:
I want to start with the distinction that matters most, because everything else on this page depends on it.

A gluten-free crust means the crust was made without gluten-containing ingredients. It does not mean the pizza was made in a gluten-free environment. At a pizza chain, those two things are very far apart, and the chains themselves are generally clear about it in their own allergen documentation — the clarity just tends to be in a footnote rather than on the menu.

Why a pizza kitchen is a difficult environment

Consider what happens in the twenty feet behind the counter. Wheat flour is used to stop dough sticking, which means it is airborne. Dough is stretched on shared surfaces. The same cutting wheel goes through every pizza. Pizzas travel through the same conveyor oven, where crumbs from earlier bakes remain. Staff handle wheat dough and then handle your toppings.

A store can put a certified gluten-free base into that environment and it will pick up trace gluten. That is not negligence; it is a physical property of the room. Eliminating it would require a separate prep area, separate utensils, separate oven and separate staff — which is why the restaurants that can genuinely serve coeliac customers are dedicated gluten-free kitchens, and a pizza chain is not one.

What that means for you, specifically

The right answer depends on why you avoid gluten.

If you have coeliac disease

Most chains state directly that they do not recommend their gluten-free crust for people with coeliac disease. Take that at face value. It is not a legal hedge on a product that would actually be fine; it is an accurate description of the kitchen.

The amount of gluten that triggers an immune response in coeliac disease is very small, and trace cross-contact in a flour-heavy kitchen is realistically unavoidable. A dedicated gluten-free kitchen, or cooking at home, is the safer route.

If you have non-coeliac gluten sensitivity

This is where individual tolerance genuinely varies. Some people find a chain gluten-free crust perfectly manageable; others react to the trace exposure. Only you can calibrate that, and the honest advice is to try it once when the consequences of being wrong are low rather than before an important day.

If you are avoiding gluten by preference

Then trace cross-contact is not a health concern and the crust is simply a menu choice. Order it if you prefer it.

If you have a wheat allergy

Treat this with the same caution as coeliac disease, or more. An allergic reaction can be triggered by trace exposure and the consequences are acute rather than cumulative.

The practical details

Size. Gluten-free bases are usually available in one size only, most often a small or medium. Planning to feed a group from one is not realistic.

Price. A few dollars above a standard base, and frequently excluded from deal pricing or surcharged inside it. Assume it will not be covered by whatever offer you were planning to use.

Texture. Denser and crisper than wheat dough, with a firmer bite. It is a reasonable product judged on its own terms and a poor one judged as an imitation of a hand-tossed base.

Toppings. Most are gluten-free, but seasoned meats and some sauces can contain wheat-based binders or thickeners. This varies by chain and by supplier, and suppliers change. Request current allergen information rather than relying on a list you read a year ago.

Reducing risk if you order anyway

If you have decided the risk level suits you, these help at the margins:

  • Order at a quiet time. A kitchen at 6:30pm on a Friday has more airborne flour and more time pressure than the same kitchen at 3pm on a Tuesday.
  • State the reason. Saying it is for a medical requirement rather than a preference prompts staff to change gloves and use a clean cutter at most stores.
