  • Ask for it uncut. The shared cutting wheel is a documented cross-contact point, and cutting it yourself at home removes it entirely.
  • Keep the toppings simple. Fewer ingredients means fewer opportunities for a wheat-containing component to be present.

The bottom line

Chain gluten-free crusts are a real product that fills a real need for people avoiding gluten by preference or with mild sensitivity. For coeliac disease and wheat allergy, the chains' own guidance says not to rely on them, and that guidance is correct.

The crust is gluten-free. The kitchen is not. Which one matters more depends entirely on you.

Reading a chain's own allergen documentation

If you are going to rely on anything, rely on the chain's own allergen statement rather than on a menu description or a summary like this one. A few things to look for when you do.

Check the date on the document. Supplier changes happen, formulations get revised, and an allergen sheet that has not been updated in two years is describing a kitchen that may no longer exist.

Look for the language about preparation environment specifically, not just about ingredients. A statement that a crust contains no gluten ingredients and a statement that a crust is safe for coeliac disease are very different claims, and most chains are careful to make only the first one. That carefulness is informative.

Check whether the statement covers the whole order or only the crust. Toppings, sauces and dips are frequently documented separately.

What has actually improved

It is worth acknowledging that gluten-free options at chains are better than they were. A decade ago the choice was frequently nothing at all; now most major chains carry a base that is a reasonable product rather than an apology.

What has not changed, and structurally cannot without a separate kitchen, is the cross-contact question. That is a building problem rather than a recipe problem, and no amount of supplier improvement addresses it.

So the honest summary is that the ingredient side of this has largely been solved and the environment side has not. Which of those matters to you determines whether the option is useful or irrelevant, and that is a decision only you can make.

title: Vegetarian and Vegan Pizza: What Is Available
excerpt: Vegetarian is straightforward at most pizza chains. Vegan is not, and the reason is the cheese — plus a couple of ingredients people rarely think to check.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Photo for a guide to vegetarian and vegan pizza options

faqs.question: Is chain pizza dough vegan?
faqs.answer: The standard dough at most chains is made without animal ingredients, but stuffed, buttered and some flavoured crusts frequently contain dairy. Verify the specific crust rather than assuming that dough in general is safe.

faqs.question: Do pizza chains offer vegan cheese?
faqs.answer: Some stores stock a plant-based cheese alternative and many do not, and availability varies by region and even by individual store. Check your own store's menu before planning an order around it.

faqs.question: Is the tomato pizza sauce vegetarian?
faqs.answer: Standard tomato pizza sauce usually is, but creamy and alfredo-style sauces contain dairy, and some barbecue and specialty sauces contain animal-derived ingredients. The base sauce is the item most worth checking after the cheese.

content:
Ordering vegetarian at a pizza chain is easy. Ordering vegan is a research project. The gap between those two experiences is almost entirely about cheese, with a few smaller traps around the edges.

Vegetarian: mostly straightforward

Every chain menu has at least one vegetable pizza, and any pizza can have its meat removed at no charge — removal is free where addition is not, which is worth remembering generally.

Two things are still worth checking.

The cheese. Some cheeses are made with animal rennet and some with microbial rennet. Which one a chain uses varies by supplier and can vary by region within the same chain. If you avoid animal rennet, this needs confirming rather than assuming.

The dough conditioner. Some commercial dough formulations include ingredients that are not vegetarian. This is uncommon but not unheard of, and it is not something you can determine by looking at the pizza.

For most people ordering vegetarian by preference rather than by strict rule, the vegetable pizzas on any chain menu are fine and this level of checking is unnecessary. For anyone who does need certainty, ask the chain for their current ingredient information — the answer changes when suppliers change.

Vegan: considerably harder

The core problem is that pizza is a cheese delivery system, and removing the cheese leaves you with sauce on bread.

Cheese alternatives

Availability is genuinely inconsistent. Some stores stock a plant-based cheese, many do not, and it varies by region and sometimes store to store within the same city. This is the single item to confirm before building an order — discovering at checkout that your store does not carry it is a common and annoying experience.

Where it is unavailable, a no-cheese pizza with a generous topping load and extra sauce is a legitimate order that a lot of vegan customers make. Ask for well done: without cheese acting as a moisture barrier, the base benefits from extra oven time.

The dough

Standard pizza dough at most chains is made without animal ingredients. The exceptions cluster in the specialty crusts — stuffed crusts, buttered rims and some flavoured bases frequently contain dairy.

The garlic butter brushed onto breadsticks and pizza rims after baking is a specific and easily-missed one. It is often genuine dairy butter.

The sauces

Standard tomato sauce is usually fine. Creamy and alfredo-style sauces are not. Some barbecue and specialty sauces contain animal-derived ingredients, most often honey or dairy solids.

The sides

Most bread sides carry cheese, butter or both. Plain breadsticks may be brushed with dairy butter even without a cheese topping. Desserts almost always contain dairy and egg. The sides section is where vegan orders most often come unstuck, because the pizza itself got all the attention.

A realistic vegan order

What actually works at most chains:

  • Standard hand-tossed or thin crust base, confirmed dairy-free.
  • Standard tomato sauce, ordered extra.
  • Plant-based cheese if stocked; no cheese if not.
  • A heavy vegetable load — mushrooms, peppers, onions, olives, tomato — since without cheese the toppings carry the whole pizza.
  • Well done.
  • Skip the sides, or check each one individually rather than assuming.

On cross-contact

The same principle applies here as with gluten: a pizza kitchen is a shared environment. The same surfaces, cutters and oven handle meat and dairy all day.

For most people avoiding animal products by ethical or dietary preference, this is not a health issue and is generally accepted as unavoidable in a non-vegan kitchen. For anyone with a dairy allergy, it is a genuine safety consideration and should be treated the way any allergy is — trace exposure is possible and a chain pizza kitchen cannot rule it out.

Where the industry is going

Plant-based cheese availability at chains has broadened over recent years but remains patchy, and it is the constraint on everything else. The vegetable toppings have always been there; the dough is usually fine; the missing piece has consistently been a cheese that melts acceptably and that stores are willing to stock.

Until availability becomes consistent, the practical advice is unchanged: check your specific store first, and build the order around what it actually carries rather than what the national menu suggests.

Ordering a good no-cheese pizza

If your store does not stock a plant-based cheese, a no-cheese pizza is the fallback, and it can be genuinely good rather than merely acceptable — but only if you order it deliberately.

Cheese does two jobs on a pizza beyond taste: it binds the toppings to the base and it acts as a moisture barrier. Remove it and both jobs go unfilled, which is why a plain no-cheese pizza often arrives as a dry base with toppings sliding off it.

Three adjustments fix most of that. Ask for extra sauce, which restores moisture and gives the toppings something to sit in. Ask for well done, since without cheese insulating the base it can take more oven time comfortably. And load the toppings heavily — with no cheese to carry the pizza, the vegetables have to do all the work.

A drizzle of oil after it arrives, and something acidic on the table, closes most of the remaining gap.

What to ask when you call

If you need to check ingredients with a store rather than relying on published information, asking about specific items gets a far better answer than asking whether something is vegan. Staff answer that second question inconsistently because it depends on definitions they were never trained on.

Useful questions: does the dough contain any dairy or animal-derived ingredient; is the garlic butter on the breadsticks real butter; is the standard tomato sauce dairy-free; do you stock a plant-based cheese today. Four concrete answers beat one vague reassurance.

title: Pizza Calories: Which Choices Actually Change the Number
excerpt: Some pizza decisions move the calorie count substantially and some barely register. Here is which is which, ranked by impact.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Photo for a guide to pizza calories and nutrition
keywords: how many calories in a slice of pizza

pricing.label: Calories per slice, large pizza
pricing.note: Thin crust cheese at the low end, pan crust with multiple meats at the high end. Same order, same store.

faqs.question: How many calories are in a slice of pizza?
faqs.answer: Roughly 140 to 340 for a slice of a large pizza, depending mostly on crust and toppings. Thin crust cheese sits at the bottom of that range and pan crust with several meat toppings at the top — a difference of more than double from the same menu.

faqs.question: What is the biggest calorie saving on a chain pizza?
faqs.answer: Switching to thin crust, which removes roughly a third of the base calories while leaving the toppings and cheese untouched. It is free at most stores, which makes it the largest no-cost reduction available.

faqs.question: Does light cheese make a meaningful difference?
faqs.answer: Yes — cheese is one of the largest single contributors on a pizza, and requesting light cheese is a free modification at most stores. Combined with thin crust it can take a slice down substantially without removing a topping.

content:
Pizza has a reputation as a single monolithic unhealthy food, which is not a useful way to think about it. A slice of thin-crust vegetable pizza and a slice of pan-crust meat pizza differ by more than double in calories, and they came from the same menu.

Here is what actually moves the number, in order of how much it moves it.

1. The crust — the largest single lever

Per slice of a large pizza, before any toppings:

  • Thin crust: around 140 calories
  • Hand tossed: around 200 calories
  • Pan: around 280 calories

Switching from pan to thin crust removes roughly 140 calories per slice with the toppings unchanged. Across three slices, that is more than a full slice of pizza's worth.

What makes this the most useful intervention is that it is free and it removes nothing you wanted. Nobody orders a pizza for the dough.

2. Cheese

Cheese is the second-largest contributor and one of the few that is both substantial and free to reduce. Light cheese is a no-charge modification at most stores.

Extra cheese, correspondingly, is one of the largest paid increases available — it is also, as we have argued elsewhere, one of the weakest paid modifications on the menu in terms of what you actually notice. It costs money and calories for a difference that is often invisible.

3. Meat toppings

Roughly 30 to 40 calories per slice per meat topping on a large. A pizza with four meats is carrying something like 120 to 160 additional calories per slice over a plain one.

Vegetable toppings, by contrast, add around 5 to 15 calories per slice. Loading a pizza with vegetables changes the calorie count very little and improves the pizza considerably, which makes it one of the better trades on the menu.

4. How many slices you eat

Not a menu decision, but it dominates all of the above.

Three slices of a heavy pan pizza is around a thousand calories. Three slices of a thin-crust vegetable pizza is around five hundred. But six slices of the thin-crust pizza is a thousand again, and a lighter pizza is easier to eat six slices of.

I mention this because the practical failure mode of ordering the lighter option is eating more of it. If that is your pattern, ordering a smaller pizza is more effective than ordering a lighter one.

5. Sides and drinks — the invisible half

This is where people are most often surprised.

  • A piece of cheesy bread is comparable to a slice of pizza.
  • A single-serving baked pasta is comparable to three slices.
  • Two lava cakes come to roughly 800 calories.
  • A regular soft drink adds around 100 calories per glass, and a two-litre bottle across an evening adds up quickly.

People carefully choose a thin crust and then order cheesy bread, pasta and dessert alongside it. The pizza was never the largest item on that order.

What a lighter chain pizza order looks like

Not a diet plan — just the same order, built with the free levers pulled:

  • Thin crust.
  • Light cheese.
  • One meat topping rather than three, plus as many vegetables as you like.
  • Well done, which does not change the calories but does improve a thin-crust vegetable pizza considerably.
  • Water or a zero-sugar drink.
  • Skip the bread side, or share one.

Against a pan-crust meat pizza with cheesy bread and soda, that is a difference of several hundred calories per person. Nothing on the list involves eating less pizza — it involves choosing differently at points where the choice was free anyway.

Some perspective

The honest take: we'd rather someone ordered pizza they enjoyed once a week than felt bad about it. The numbers on this page are for making informed choices, not for making anyone anxious about dinner.

The two genuinely useful facts are these: the crust is the biggest lever and it is free, and the sides are a bigger contributor than most people realise. Everything else is detail.

A note on the figures

All numbers here are approximate and vary by chain, region and store. Portioning at a chain store is done by hand against a target, so two pizzas built to the same specification can differ. Where a chain publishes its own nutrition information, treat that as authoritative over any general guide including this one.

Why published figures and your pizza differ

A short note on precision, because the numbers on this page look more exact than they are.

Portioning at a chain store is done by hand against a target. A generous shift and a light-handed one produce visibly different pizzas from the same specification, and cheese in particular varies more than most people would guess. Published nutrition figures describe the specification, not the pizza in front of you.

That variation is not a reason to ignore the numbers — the difference between a thin-crust vegetable pizza and a pan meat pizza dwarfs any portioning variance. It is a reason not to treat a fifteen-calorie difference between two options as meaningful. Use the figures for the big decisions and ignore them for the small ones.

What actually helps, if you order regularly

Three habits, in order of how much difference they make for someone eating chain pizza most weeks:

  • Decide how many slices before the box opens. This dominates every menu choice on this page. Portioning onto a plate rather than eating from the box is unglamorous and effective.
  • Default to thin crust unless you have a reason not to. It is free, it removes nothing you wanted, and over a month of regular ordering it adds up substantially.
  • Treat the sides as food, not as extras. Cheesy bread and a baked pasta alongside a pizza is two meals arriving as one, and it is where most of the surprise in a takeaway calorie count lives.

None of that involves eating pizza less often, which is deliberate. Advice you will not follow is not advice.

title: How Much to Tip a Pizza Delivery Driver
excerpt: Percentage rules break down on small orders. Here is a framework that holds up across order sizes, weather and distance.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Photo for a guide to tipping pizza delivery drivers
keywords: how much to tip pizza delivery

faqs.question: What is a standard tip for pizza delivery?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to twenty percent of the food total is the common benchmark, with a floor of three to five dollars on small orders. The floor matters because the driving effort is identical whether the order is ten dollars or forty.

faqs.question: Should I tip more in bad weather?
faqs.answer: Yes. Snow, ice and heavy rain make each run slower and more dangerous, which reduces how many deliveries a driver can complete across a whole shift. A few extra dollars is a reasonable acknowledgement of that.

faqs.question: Do I still tip if there is a delivery fee?
faqs.answer: Yes. At most chains the delivery fee is a store charge covering insurance and operating costs and does not go to the driver. Reducing the tip because a fee was applied takes money from the driver, not the company.

content:
Tipping advice usually arrives as a percentage and stops there. Percentages are a reasonable starting point and they break down at both ends of the range, which is where most of the real questions live.

Here is the framework delivery drivers themselves say actually holds up.

Start with the floor, not the percentage

The work of a delivery is almost identical whether your order is ten dollars or forty. Same drive, same parking, same stairs, same conversation at the door. The only thing that scales with order size is how heavy the bag is.

So a pure percentage under-pays badly on small orders. Fifteen percent of a twelve-dollar order is a dollar eighty for a fifteen-minute round trip, which is not a serious number.

Start at three to five dollars as a minimum, then apply a percentage on top for larger orders. On anything above roughly twenty-five dollars, fifteen to twenty percent will exceed the floor naturally and the percentage takes over.

Adjust for the things that cost the driver time

Time is the driver's actual currency. Tips per hour is what determines whether a shift was worth working, so anything that slows a run down reduces income across the whole night, not just on your delivery.

Add for bad weather. Snow, ice and heavy rain slow every run and make several of them genuinely unpleasant. A few extra dollars is warranted and it is noticed.

Add for distance. If you are at the edge of a delivery zone, your order is a twenty-five minute round trip rather than an eight minute one. That is two runs the driver did not do.

Add for difficulty. Fourth-floor walk-up, gated complex with a code that does not work, long unlit driveway, an apartment block where the numbering makes no sense. All of it is unpaid time.

Add for a large or awkward order. Six pizzas and four two-litre bottles is two trips from the car.

The fee is not the tip

I have written about this at length elsewhere, so briefly: at most chains the delivery fee goes to the store, not the driver. It covers insurance, vehicle costs and operational overhead.

When someone reduces a tip because they have already paid a delivery fee, the reduction comes out of the driver's income and the chain's revenue is unchanged. It is the most common tipping mistake I encountered and it was never made maliciously — the checkout screen simply does not explain it.

Cash or card

Both reach the driver at a chain store. There is a stubborn rumour that card tips get skimmed, and at chain stores it is not true.

The real difference is timing: cash is in their pocket that night, a card tip arrives in a future payslip. If you have cash, it is slightly better. If you do not, tip on the card without worrying about it.

When a lower tip is reasonable

Tipping is not unconditional and I would not argue that it is. A genuinely poor delivery — wrong order, obvious rudeness, food clearly mishandled — is a fair reason to tip less.

But be sure the fault is the driver's. Things that are not:

  • The food was cold after a long journey. That is distance and queue depth.
  • The order was wrong. Assembled in the kitchen, not by the driver, who does not open the box.
  • It took an hour on a Friday night. That is the store's queue. The driver delivered it as soon as it existed.
  • The tracker said twenty minutes and it took forty. The tracker is an estimate produced by a system, not a promise made by a person.

Almost everything that goes wrong with a delivery order happens before the driver picks up the bag.

If money is tight

Fair enough, and there are better places to cut. Switch to carryout if the store is close — no delivery, no fee, no tip owed, and usually a cheaper pizza. Drop the drinks. Order from a bundle. Skip the paid extras.

All of those save more than trimming a tip does, and none of them come out of someone's wages.

The rule I would give a friend

Five dollars minimum. Twenty percent on anything substantial. More in the snow, more up stairs, more at the edge of the zone. And do not subtract for the delivery fee, because that money never reached the person standing at your door.

Tipping in advance versus at the door

A question worth addressing: does tipping when you place the order change the service you get?

Not at a chain store, and this is one of the clearer differences between chain delivery and gig-economy platforms. On an app where drivers see the payout before accepting a job, a low tip can genuinely mean your order sits unclaimed. At a chain, a salaried or hourly driver is handed a run by dispatch and delivers what they are given, in the order they are given it. Nobody is declining your delivery because of the tip.

What that means practically is that tipping at checkout and tipping at the door are equivalent in outcome. Choose whichever you find easier — though a card tip entered at checkout is one fewer thing to think about when the doorbell goes.

Group orders and large deliveries

Large orders deserve a specific mention because percentage-based tipping starts to look uncomfortable at the top end.

Twenty percent on a hundred-dollar party order is twenty dollars for one delivery, which is high by any measure. But that order is also two trips from the car, likely a scheduled slot the store worked around, and often a walk into a building rather than a doorstep handover.

Somewhere in the ten to fifteen percent range on very large orders, with a floor well above what a small order would earn, is where most people land and where I would land too. The principle is the same as everywhere else on this page: pay for the work, not for the food.

title: Ordering Pizza for a Group: How Much to Get
excerpt: The two mistakes are ordering too little and ordering the wrong shape of deal. Both are avoidable with about five minutes of planning.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Photo for a guide to ordering pizza for a group
keywords: how many pizzas for a group

faqs.question: How many pizzas do I need for 10 people?
faqs.answer: Three to four large pizzas, depending on whether there are sides. The working rule is three slices per adult when pizza is the whole meal and two when there are sides, against eight slices per large pizza.

faqs.question: Is a party bundle better than ordering individually?
faqs.answer: Usually on price, but it dictates the composition. A multi-slot mix and match often lands at a similar total while letting you choose exactly what goes in, so it is worth pricing both before committing.

faqs.question: How far ahead should I order for a large group?
faqs.answer: Ninety minutes on a weekend evening, and use the scheduled ordering function. Large orders are sequenced around smaller ones during a rush, so scheduling protects your place in the queue rather than leaving you at the back of it.

content:
Ordering pizza for ten people is a different problem from ordering for two, and the failure modes are specific: not enough food, the wrong deal structure, and food that arrives forty minutes after you needed it.

All three are solvable in advance.

How much food you actually need

The working numbers, from planning a lot of these:

  • Pizza as the whole meal: three slices per adult.
  • Pizza with sides on the table: two slices per adult.
  • Children: one to two slices.
  • A large pizza: eight slices. An extra-large: ten.

So for ten adults with sides, that is twenty slices, which is three large pizzas with a little spare. For ten adults with no sides, thirty slices, which is four larges.

Round up rather than down. Leftover pizza is a known and welcome quantity; running out in front of guests is not.

Which deal structure suits a group

Two candidates, and they are closer than people assume.

The family or party bundle

A fixed composition — typically four pizzas plus sides plus a drink — at one price. Lowest cost per head of anything on the menu.

The catch is that the composition is fixed, and specialty pizzas frequently carry a surcharge of a dollar or two each inside the bundle. On a four-pizza order that is meaningful.

Multi-slot mix and match

Most two-item bundles extend to more items at the same flat rate. Four pizzas at the flat rate is often within a few dollars of a party pack, and you control the composition completely.

Price both. They land close together often enough that the five minutes is worthwhile, and the mix and match usually wins if your group has specific requirements.

What to order for a mixed group

The composition that reliably works for ten to twelve people:

  • One plain cheese. There is always someone. Children, in particular.
  • One pepperoni. The most-ordered pizza in the country; it will disappear first.
  • One vegetable. Covers vegetarians and the people who wanted something lighter.
  • One loaded meat or specialty. For the people who came to eat.

Half-and-half pizzas are worth knowing about here: most chains charge the price of the more expensive half rather than a premium, so two half-and-half pizzas cover four preferences at the cost of two pizzas.

Sides, honestly assessed

For a group, bread sides are the efficient choice — cheap, filling, universally acceptable, and they reduce how much pizza each person eats, which lets you order one fewer pizza.

Wings are the inefficient choice. Substantial bone weight, and at four to five wings per person for a group of ten you are ordering two large portions to serve as a side dish.

Drinks: buy them from a shop. Two litres from a pizza store costs roughly double supermarket price, and on a party order that is ten or fifteen dollars of pure convenience charge.

The timing, which matters more than the order

This is where group orders actually fail.

Order ninety minutes ahead on a weekend evening. Large orders are sequenced around smaller ones during a rush — a store will not stop making twenty ordinary pizzas to build your four at once. Scheduling puts you in the queue deliberately rather than at the back of it by accident.

Use the scheduled ordering function. It exists, it is underused, and it converts a large order from a gamble into an appointment.

Consider carryout for very large orders. The saving scales with order size, and a store will have four pizzas boxed and waiting at a scheduled time. Sending one person to collect is often the single biggest saving available on a party order.

Add fifteen minutes to whatever the tracker says if you are ordering into a Friday or Saturday peak, and plan the evening around the later number.

A worked example: twelve people

  • Four large pizzas — cheese, pepperoni, vegetable, meat — at roughly twenty-four slices with sides on the table.
  • Two large orders of breadsticks or cheesy bread.
  • Drinks from the supermarket.
  • Priced under both a party bundle and a four-slot mix and match, taking whichever is lower.
  • Scheduled ninety minutes ahead, collected if someone can drive.

That feeds twelve people comfortably, arrives when you asked for it, and costs meaningfully less than the same food ordered at seven o'clock on the night with drinks added at the till.

Handling dietary requirements without doubling the order

Almost every group has at least one person who cannot eat the default pizza, and the instinct is to order them a separate small one. That is usually the most expensive way to solve it.

Half-and-half is the cheaper structure. At most chains a half-and-half pizza costs the price of the more expensive half rather than carrying a premium, so one pizza can cover a vegetarian and a meat eater at no additional cost. Two half-and-half larges cover four requirements for the price of two pizzas.

Gluten-free is the exception, because those bases usually come in one size only and cannot sensibly be shared. If someone in the group needs one, order it as a genuinely separate item and read our guide on what a chain gluten-free crust does and does not mean before you do.

The mistake nobody expects

Ordering everything cold-tolerant and nothing hot-tolerant. If your food is arriving forty minutes before people eat — which is common at a party, where the food arrives before the guests are ready — the composition matters more than the quantity.

Pizza holds up reasonably. Boneless chicken holds up well. Breadsticks harden within half an hour. Cheesy bread sets and changes texture. Lava cakes lose their molten centre entirely.

For a party where the food will sit, weight the order toward pizza and chicken, and either skip the temperature-sensitive items or schedule them to arrive with a second, later delivery. Ordering four lava cakes ninety minutes before anyone eats dessert is money spent on a product you will not receive.

title: Late-Night Pizza: What's Open After 10pm
excerpt: Closing time and last-order time are different things, and the gap between them catches people out constantly.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Photo for a guide to late-night pizza hours

faqs.question: What time do pizza chains stop delivering?
faqs.answer: Most stores stop accepting delivery orders twenty to thirty minutes before their posted closing time, so a store closing at midnight typically takes its last delivery order around 11:30pm. Carryout is often accepted slightly later than delivery.

faqs.question: Are pizza stores open later at weekends?
faqs.answer: Usually by an hour or so on Friday and Saturday. Hours are set store by store rather than nationally, so the store two miles away can genuinely close an hour later than yours.

faqs.question: Is the food different late at night?
faqs.answer: The recipe is identical, but the last hour of trading is when the kitchen is being cleaned down and staffing is at its lowest. Ordering thirty minutes before close rather than five minutes before it makes a noticeable difference.

content:
The most common late-night pizza mistake is assuming that a store listed as closing at midnight will take an order at 11:55pm. It will not, and the reason is straightforward once you have worked a closing shift.

Closing time is not last-order time

The posted closing time is when the store shuts. The last order has to be taken, made, baked, boxed and — for delivery — driven to you and back, all before that.

In practice most stores stop accepting delivery orders twenty to thirty minutes before close. A midnight close usually means a last delivery order around 11:30pm.

Carryout often runs slightly later, because there is no round trip to fit in. If you are close to the wire, switching to collection sometimes buys you fifteen minutes.

Hours are set per store, not nationally

Franchisees set their own hours based on local demand and staffing. This means the chain's general hours are guidance rather than fact, and two stores in the same city can differ by more than an hour.

Always check your specific store after entering your address. The national page will tell you what is typical; your store page tells you what is true.

Typical patterns

Across the markets we track, the general shape:

  • Weeknights: most stores close between 11pm and midnight.
  • Friday and Saturday: usually an hour later, midnight to 1am.
  • Sunday: often the earliest close of the week.
  • Campus and city-centre stores: consistently later than suburban ones, because the demand justifies the staffing.

If late-night ordering is a regular thing for you, it is worth finding out which store near you keeps the latest hours once, rather than checking every time.

What actually changes in the last hour

The recipe does not change. The circumstances do.

Staffing is at its lowest. The closing crew is smaller than the dinner-rush crew, so a burst of late orders takes longer to clear than the same volume at 7pm.

Clean-down has started. Prep areas and equipment are being broken down and cleaned progressively through the last hour. That is a health requirement, not laziness, and it means a late order is being made around a partially disassembled line.

Some items may be unavailable. Where an item requires equipment that has already been cleaned, it can quietly drop off availability. Wings and pasta are the usual candidates.

Delivery zones sometimes shrink. With fewer drivers on, some stores restrict how far they will send a late run.

None of this makes a late-night pizza bad. It does mean that ordering at 11pm rather than 11:28pm gets you a noticeably better experience for no extra cost.

Late-night deals

Some stores run late-night offers — a discounted pizza and side combo after a certain hour — designed to keep the kitchen busy in the slow period before close.

These are almost always store-level rather than national. If it is not showing on your store's deals page, your store is not running it, and no code will make it appear.

Practical advice

  • Check your specific store's hours, not the chain's general ones.
  • Assume the last order is thirty minutes before close and work backwards from there.
  • Order at 11pm rather than 11:30pm if you have the choice. Better food, less pressure on the kitchen, and no risk of missing the cut-off.
  • Try carryout if you have missed the delivery window. It sometimes runs later.
  • Tip well on a late run. A driver on the last delivery of the night is finishing their shift with your order and going back to clean down.

If you have missed it entirely

Once the store is closed, it is closed — there is no back door, and calling will not reach anyone. The realistic options are a twenty-four-hour store if your city has one, or scheduling an order for tomorrow, which most chains allow you to do at any hour.

The scheduling option is genuinely useful and almost nobody uses it: you can place tomorrow's lunch order at 1am when you discover the store is shut.

Why hours differ so much between nearby stores

Two stores three miles apart can close an hour apart, and the reason is entirely economic rather than corporate.

Staying open costs a franchisee real money: staff on the clock, ovens running, lights on, a driver available. That is only worth doing if the late hour generates enough orders to cover it. A store next to a university or in a city centre with late-night trade clears that bar easily. A suburban store where the last order comes in at ten does not, and closing earlier is a rational decision rather than a service failure.

Which is why the answer to what time does pizza close is always store-specific, and why the national page can only ever tell you what is typical.

Ordering ahead, which almost nobody does

The scheduling function on most chain sites is one of the more useful features nobody uses, and it is particularly useful at the ends of the day.

You can place an order at one in the morning for delivery at midday tomorrow. If you have just discovered your store is closed, that is a better outcome than nothing — the order is locked in, and lunch is handled before you have got out of bed.

It also solves the opposite problem. If you know you will want food at eleven tonight and your store's last delivery order is at half past eleven, scheduling removes the risk of remembering at twenty-five past and finding the store has stopped taking orders early because the closing crew is already breaking down the line.

title: What the Pizza Tracker Is Actually Telling You
excerpt: The tracker is a real status display for part of the process and an estimate for the rest. Knowing which stage is which explains most of its inaccuracy.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Photo explaining how the pizza order tracker works

faqs.question: Is the pizza tracker accurate?
faqs.answer: The in-store stages are driven by real events staff log at the point of sale, so they are broadly accurate. The delivery stage is where accuracy drops, because it starts from a real event — the driver leaving — and then estimates the rest.

faqs.question: Why does the tracker say delivered before the food arrives?
faqs.answer: At many stores the driver marks the run complete when they leave the vehicle or as they finish the drop, so the status can update a minute or two before the doorbell rings. It is a timing artefact rather than an error.

faqs.question: Does the tracker show the driver's live location?
faqs.answer: Some chains now offer live GPS tracking on the delivery leg; many still show a stage indicator with an estimate instead. Which one you get depends on the chain and sometimes on the individual store's equipment.

content:
The order tracker is one of the more successful pieces of interface design in fast food, and it is widely misunderstood. It is not a lie, and it is also not a live feed. It is a mix of both, and knowing which stage is which explains almost every complaint people have about it.

What each stage actually is

Order placed

Real and instant. Your order hit the store's point-of-sale system.

Prep

Real. Someone marked it as started at the make line, or the system did when it was routed there. This stage is genuine.

Bake

Mostly real, and this is the most reliable stage on the whole tracker. Conveyor ovens run at a fixed speed, so a pizza that enters takes a known number of minutes to come out. When the tracker says bake, it is accurate to within about a minute.

Quality check / boxing

Real but brief. Marked when the pizza is boxed. In a busy store this stage can pass in seconds, which is why it sometimes seems to be skipped entirely.

Out for delivery

The transition is real — a driver logged your order onto their run. Everything after that is an estimate.

This is where the accuracy drops, and it drops for a specific reason: the driver almost certainly has more than one order in the car.

Why your delivery takes longer than the estimate

Drivers run multiple deliveries per trip. It is not a cost-saving trick; it is how the job has always worked, and it is what makes delivery economically viable at all.

So when the tracker says out for delivery, your pizza might be first on a run of three or last. If it is last, it has been in the car for two other stops before it reaches you. The tracker generally cannot show that, because it is displaying your order's status, not the driver's route.

Some chains now offer live GPS on the delivery leg, which solves this by showing you where the car actually is. Where that exists it is a genuine improvement. Where it does not, the delivery estimate is a model.

Why it sometimes says delivered before it arrives

Depending on the store's system, the driver marks the run complete either when they leave the vehicle or as they finish the handover. Either way the status can update a minute or two before your doorbell rings.

Not an error, just an artefact of when the button gets pressed.

The staff names

The name shown at each stage is usually a real person clocked into that station. It is not always the person who physically handled your pizza — in a busy kitchen, whoever is logged into the terminal gets attributed — but there is a real employee behind the name.

What the tracker will not tell you

This is the useful part.

How deep the queue is. Your order sitting at prep for twelve minutes on a Friday means there are fifteen orders in front of it. The tracker shows your stage, not your position.

How many stops are ahead of you. As above.

That something has gone wrong. If an order is remade after a mistake, the tracker frequently does not reset to show it. The stage indicator can sit on delivery while a replacement pizza is being baked.

Whether the store is short-staffed. Which is the single biggest driver of a slow night and is invisible in every version of this interface.

How to read it usefully

  • Trust the bake stage. It is genuinely accurate and it means your food exists.
  • Treat the delivery estimate as optimistic at peak times. Add ten to fifteen minutes on a Friday or Saturday evening.
  • A long prep stage means a queue, not a problem. Nothing is wrong; there are simply orders ahead of yours.
  • Call the store if it has been stuck for a long time. Twenty minutes on one stage with no movement is worth a phone call, and phone staff can see the actual order record rather than the customer-facing summary.

Why it exists at all

Honestly? Because waiting with information is much more tolerable than waiting without it. The tracker did not make pizza arrive faster; it made the same wait feel manageable, and it substantially reduced the number of people phoning stores to ask where their order was.

That is a real product improvement even though nothing about the pizza changed. Just do not mistake the delivery estimate for a promise — the in-store stages are a status display, and the last one is a forecast.

What to do when the tracker stalls

A practical decision tree, since this is the situation people actually find themselves in.

Stuck at prep for more than fifteen minutes. Almost certainly a queue. Frustrating, not broken. On a Friday evening this is normal and calling will not move you up the list.

Stuck at bake for more than ten minutes. Unusual, because bake is the one genuinely time-boxed stage. This more often means the order was remade after a problem and the tracker did not reset. Worth a call.

Out for delivery for more than forty minutes. You are probably last on a multi-stop run, or your address is at the edge of the zone. If it passes an hour, call — occasionally an order gets marked out and left behind.

Marked delivered but nothing arrived. Call immediately rather than waiting. The most common causes are a neighbouring address or a drop-off at a door you do not use, and both are much easier to resolve in the first ten minutes.

Why phoning the store beats phoning anyone else

Store staff can see the actual order record: which driver has it, how many stops are on that run, whether it was remade. The customer-facing tracker is a summary of that record, and a lossy one.

Corporate customer service, by contrast, generally cannot see live store operations at all and will end up calling the store on your behalf. Going straight to the store removes a step and gets you the person who can actually look at the screen that matters.
